text:
China's K-culture ban ease offers new opportunities but competition looms Korean entertainment and consumer brands are poised to gain greater access to China under a new trade agreement, but they face tougher local competition than when Beijing first restricted Korean cultural exports nearly a decade ago, market watchers said Thursday.
Seoul and Beijing agreed Wednesday to expand their free trade agreement to cover services and investment after more than eight years of talks. The deal could boost bilateral services trade, which has long lagged behind merchandise trade.
The entertainment industry stands to be among the biggest beneficiaries. China was the world's second-largest content market in 2024 and was growing faster than the U.S. market, according to the Korea Creative Content Agency.
With K-pop enjoying a far stronger global following than before the restrictions, easing barriers could bring more live concerts to China, expand Korean music's presence on Chinese streaming platforms and open doors for Korean game developers.
The potential reopening follows years of strained economic ties between the two neighbors.
Korean companies invested heavily in China after the latter joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, helping transform the country into a manufacturing powerhouse while boosting productivity at home.
Relations soured after Seoul deployed the U.S. Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile system in 2017, prompting Beijing to impose unofficial restrictions on Korean popular culture, known as the Korean wave.
"Korean content has faced significant restrictions in China," said Troy Stangarone, a non-resident fellow at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology. "But issues with piracy and local reproductions of Korean content demonstrate that there is still strong demand."
Yet Korean companies face a markedly different Chinese market from the one they left behind.
Chinese dramas are gaining audiences on global streaming platforms such as Netflix, while domestic game developers have strengthened their capabilities and found success overseas.
"Beijing has consistently denied the existence of any formal restrictions on Korean cultural content. The mere fact that regulatory easing has been explicitly written into the agreement carries considerable significance," said Lee Ki-hoon, an analyst at Hana Securities. "The eased restrictions, however, largely target sectors where Chinese firms can already compete."
Korean cosmetics brands face a similar challenge as they seek to capitalize on improved ties with China, one of K-beauty's earliest overseas markets.
Domestic beauty brands, collectively known as C-beauty, have gained ground as Chinese consumers increasingly favor local products. They accounted for 55.7 percent of the market in 2024, according to the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency.
"Chinese beauty brands may arguably already exceed K-beauty in absolute value and consumer reach," Chloe Zhu, a consultant at Euromonitor International, earlier told The Korea Times . "The scale of local demand provides a structural advantage that few other markets can match."
Closer ties could also bring more Chinese tourists to Korea, offering a boost to sluggish domestic demand. Seoul had already eased visa requirements for group and independent travelers ahead of the agreement.
Still, more arrivals may do little to lift sales at duty-free operators, which have long relied heavily on Chinese visitors . Foreign tourists increasingly favor lower-priced products at retailers such as Daiso and Olive Young over luxury goods sold at duty-free stores, according to industry officials.
"Korean companies will need to develop products and tailored services that reflect evolving Chinese consumer preferences since the restrictions took effect," said Park So-young, a senior researcher at Korea International Trade Association.
The opening, however, cuts both ways, potentially giving Chinese companies a stronger foothold in Korea's domestic market.
Chinese e-commerce platforms, including AliExpress and Temu, are set to gain greater access to Korea's services market, with provisions allowing them to establish local subsidiaries and logistics centers. Payment services such as Alipay and travel platforms including Trip.com could also face fewer barriers.
Skepticism also remains over whether China will follow through on easing restrictions, with Korean businesses wary after their experience with the THAAD dispute.
"Korean consumers, they will make up their own minds as to what mainland Chinese content and products they want to buy and enjoy," said Sean King, senior vice president at Park Strategies. "Korean providers should beware ... that Beijing may well let in Korean content and products today – but just as soon block it again tomorrow."
